claims.text: Adding 1–2 at.% Y to MoNbTaTiW will improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance.
The Y addition will promote formation of a continuous oxide scale.
The Y addition will promote formation of an adherent oxide scale.
The oxide scale formed on the Y-modified alloy will be enriched in Y2O3.
Y segregates to the oxide/metal interface during high-temperature exposure.
Interfacial Y segregation enhances nucleation and growth of a slow-growing protective oxide.
The Y-modified oxide scale adheres better to the substrate than the scale on undoped MoNbTaTiW.
The proposed protective scale retards oxygen ingress.
Retarded oxygen ingress substantially slows oxidation relative to undoped MoNbTaTiW.
After 100 hours in static air at 1100°C, the Y-doped alloy will have lower oxidation-induced weight gain than the untreated alloy.
After the specified exposure, the Y-doped alloy will have a thinner oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
After the specified exposure, the Y-doped alloy will have a more coherent oxide scale than the untreated alloy.
After the specified exposure, the Y-doped alloy will exhibit less oxide-scale spallation than the untreated alloy.
Untreated MoNbTaTiW is expected to form a less controlled and more rapidly growing oxide scale with higher weight gain and possible spallation.
The reactive-element effect may be less pronounced or behave differently at significantly lower temperatures or different oxygen partial pressures.

contradictions.description: The experiment says that TEM/XPS will first confirm Y segregation at the oxide/metal interface and formation of a Y2O3-enriched scale, and only then subjects the samples to oxidation. The stated interface and oxidation scale are expected to form during the subsequent high-temperature exposure, so the sequence is internally inconsistent unless a separate pre-oxidized specimen set is intended.
